headline: Race Point rip on the slack: mackerel drops still finding bass, but you have to earn the window
subhead: The bay's turned warm and glassy for long stretches this week, and the bite has narrowed to short, sharp tide windows around the rips.
body_markdown:
Boats working the Race Point rip this week have been threading a narrow needle — a tide window that opens for maybe ninety minutes around the slack and then shuts like someone flipped a switch. That's how August goes out here. The bay's warmed up enough now that the big fish don't want to fight current all day, so they stack on the structure right at the transition, when the rip goes from ripping to breathing, and that's when the marks show up thick on the sounder over the gravel edges off Race Point and along Peaked Hill Bars.

Live mackerel has been the difference-maker. Snag a few off the surface schools working bait balls north of the Race — they're still around in decent numbers this week, just scattered wider than they were in June — and drop them back on a 5/0 circle hook, light egg sinker, right into the seam where the rip meets the flat green water. Bass in the mid-30s to upper-40s have come off that pattern on the last hour of the ebb into the slack, mostly in 25 to 40 feet of water. It's not a bite you can force. You sit on the drift, you let the boat ride the current down the edge, and you wait for the rod to load up instead of chasing marks around.

Bluefish have filled in the gaps nicely. Where the mackerel schools break up and scatter, the blues have been all over them, and that's produced some genuinely violent topwater windows off the outer edge of the rip and down toward Peaked Hill — poppers and metal-lip swimmers worked fast on the surface have been getting hit hard enough to leave marks in the wake. We flagged this pattern a couple weeks back — said wherever the bait concentrated, the surface blitzes would hold as long as the bunker and mackerel stayed thick and the weather stayed settled — and that's exactly what's playing out this week. Doesn't take much: a stable high, calm morning glass, and the blues show themselves fast.

Cod fishing has pushed deeper, which is normal for this point in the summer. The shallower structure around Billingsgate has gone quiet for cod — too warm, too much boat traffic pressing bait around — but reports out of the deeper humps and drop-offs toward the edge of the bay have kept a few boats in fish, jigging diamond jigs and teasers tipped with squid strips in 80 to 100 feet. It's not a numbers game right now. One or two decent cod for a morning's work is a fair result, and anybody telling you different is overselling it. If you want a better shot, fish the top of the tide when the current's still moving enough to keep the jig working but hasn't gone full sprint.

Fluke have been steady but unspectacular off Sandy Neck and down toward Barnstable, working the sandy troughs in 15 to 25 feet on the incoming tide. Standard drift rig — a 3/4-ounce bucktail tipped with a strip of squid or a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp — dragged slow along the bottom contour has been picking at keeper-class fish in the high teens to low 20-inch range, with enough shorts mixed in that you have to grind through some fish to find the ones worth keeping. Nothing to build a whole trip around, but a solid way to fill a cooler while waiting for the evening tide to set up the bass bite.

The moon's been fairly neutral this week, nothing extreme pushing the tides, which is part of why the bite has stayed so tide-dependent rather than moon-dependent — the fish are keying on the transition itself, not a big flood of current. That tends to favor patience over coverage. Running all over the bay chasing marks has burned a lot of fuel and produced less than just parking on a known rip edge and working the tide change methodically.

Looking ahead, if the bay holds this pattern of warm, settled mornings and modest tide swings, I'd expect the Race Point and Peaked Hill rips to keep producing on the slack windows through the coming week, with bluefish filling the gaps whenever bait scatters wide. The cod bite deeper off the bay edge should stay a grind-it-out proposition rather than a sure thing — worth a try if you've got the gas and patience, but I wouldn't build a trip solely around it right now. Fluke should stay steady off Sandy Neck and Barnstable as long as that sand structure keeps holding bait, though don't expect anything explosive there either. If a front comes through and stirs the bay up, that could actually help — a little turbulence tends to push bait tight to structure and can wake the bass up outside their usual slack-tide pattern. Until then, the smart play is picking one rip, working the transition tide patiently, and letting the mackerel do the talking.
